1.title: Application Delivery: CI/CD, GitOps, Helm
1.text: Welcome to Module 10: Application Delivery: C I slash C D, Git Ops and Helm. This module is in the Cloud Native Application Delivery domain, and it covers the topic called Application Delivery. By the end you will be able to do four things. Tell C I, continuous delivery and continuous deployment apart. Explain the Git Ops principles, pull versus push, and reconciliation. Compare recreate, rolling, blue green, canary, A B and shadow releases. And use Helm charts, releases and values, and Kustomize overlays.

1.title: Case Check-In: Harbor Books Ships Every Week
1.text: At Harbor Books, a Git repository holds what should run, and every change is a reviewed commit. A new storefront goes to a small share of visitors first, and is rolled back if orders drop. Staging and production run the same application with different settings. In this module you build the delivery path that does all of this.

1.title: CI, Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment
1.text: This slide is tagged archived topic. One pipeline carries three names. Continuous integration, C I, merges code changes as often as possible, and ends with a tested artifact. Continuous delivery deploys changes automatically to an acceptance environment, with tests and a way to roll back. Continuous deployment carries finished software directly to production. And C I is a prerequisite for C D. The diagram shows the pipeline from commit to production, with a bar for each span. Exam tip: C I builds and tests, delivery reaches acceptance, and deployment reaches production.

1.title: Registry, Tags and Digests
1.text: A pipeline builds an image, pushes it to a registry, and the cluster pulls it. How you name the image matters. A tag is a name that can be moved to point at a different image. A digest is a hash of the image content. It is unique to one version, and it is immutable. So deploy by digest when you need the same reference to mean the same image every time. And promote the same artifact from test to production, instead of rebuilding it. Exam tip: a tag can move, and a digest cannot.

1.title: GitOps: The Four Principles
1.text: This slide is tagged archived topic. Git Ops has four principles. Declarative: the desired state is described, not scripted. Versioned and immutable: it is stored with a complete history, for example in Git. Pulled automatically: software agents pull the desired state from the source. And continuously reconciled: agents observe the actual state and keep applying the desired state. Git is the usual source of truth, so drift, rollback and review all become Git operations. Exam tip: declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled, continuously reconciled.

1.title: Pull, Drift and Reconciliation
1.text: This slide is tagged archived topic. In Git Ops the agent pulls the desired state from the source. Nothing pushes into the cluster. The agent continuously compares the actual state with the desired state. Drift is the actual state moving away from the desired state, for example after a manual change. Reconciliation runs whenever there is a divergence, not only on a new commit. Traditional C I slash C D runs on pre-set triggers, and a push pipeline acts once and stops watching. Exam tip: pull plus continuous reconciliation is what fixes drift.

1.title: Argo CD and Flux
1.text: This slide is tagged archived topic. It is also tagged moving, because project status changes. Argo C D is a Git Ops tool for continuous delivery to Kubernetes, with declarative definitions. Flux keeps clusters in sync with sources such as Git repositories and O C I artifacts, and automates updates. Both are Git Ops tools for Kubernetes. They compare a source with the cluster, and bring the cluster into line. As of the thirtieth of October, twenty twenty-six, Argo, Flux and Helm are C N C F graduated projects. Exam tip: Argo C D and Flux are Git Ops tools, and Helm is a package manager.

1.title: Recreate, Rolling and Blue/Green
1.text: Three ways to replace a version. With recreate, all old Pods are killed first, then the new ones start, so there is downtime. A rolling update replaces Pods gradually. It is the Deployment default. With blue green, you keep two environments. The idle one is updated and tested, and then traffic is switched to it. The diagram shows a gap for recreate, an overlap for a rolling update, and a switch for blue green. Exam tip: recreate has downtime, rolling is gradual, and blue green switches whole environments.

1.title: Canary, A/B and Shadow Releases
1.text: Three ways to share traffic with a new version. A canary moves traffic gradually to the new version. You watch it, then continue or roll back. A B testing routes a set of users, chosen by H T T P headers or cookies, to the new version. A shadow release, also called mirroring, copies each request to the new version too, which suits idempotent requests. Canary and A B testing need layer seven traffic control, such as a service mesh or an ingress controller. Exam tip: canary shifts a share, A B picks users, and shadow copies requests.

1.title: Progressive Delivery with Argo Rollouts
1.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. Progressive delivery means shifting traffic gradually, measuring, and then promoting or rolling back. Argo Rollouts adds a controller and C R Ds to Kubernetes, for blue green, canary, canary analysis and progressive delivery. Flagger automates canary, A B, blue green and mirroring releases, with analysis, promotion and rollback. Both can work with ingress controllers and service meshes to shift traffic gradually, and they can read metrics to decide on automatic promotion or rollback. Exam tip: shift gradually, measure, then promote or roll back.

1.title: Helm: Charts, Releases and Values
1.text: Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a package. It holds a Chart dot Y A M L file, the default values dot Y A M L file, and a templates folder. A repository collects and shares charts. A release is one installed copy of a chart in a cluster. One chart can make many releases, as in the diagram where the same chart is installed twice. Helm merges the chart with values to produce the manifests. Exam tip: chart plus values makes a release.

2.title: Helm in Practice
2.text: Four Helm commands cover the basics. Install creates a release from a chart and values, from a file with the dash f option, or with set. Upgrade changes a release, and updates only what changed. History lists the revisions. Every install, upgrade or rollback adds one, starting at revision one. And rollback, with a release name and a revision, returns to an earlier revision. The snippet installs, upgrades, inspects and rolls back the database release, and then uninstalls it. Exam tip: a rollback adds a new revision, and it does not erase the history.

2.title: Kustomize: Bases and Overlays
2.text: Kustomize customizes template-free Y A M L, and leaves the original untouched. A base holds the common resources. An overlay adds patches for a variant, such as staging or production. It is built into kube control. Kube control kustomize shows the result, and kube control apply dash k applies it. The difference from Helm is simple. Helm uses templates and values. Kustomize patches plain Y A M L. Exam tip: Helm templates, Kustomize patches.

2.title: Promotion, Rollback and Infrastructure as Code
2.text: This slide is tagged beyond the curriculum. Promotion means the same change moves through the environments, from test to acceptance to production. For rollback you have helm rollback, kube control rollout undo, or in Git Ops a Git revert that the agent reconciles. And infrastructure as code means infrastructure is defined in files, not built by hand, so it is reproducible. Crossplane, a C N C F project, builds control planes for applications and infrastructure. Exam tip: what lives in files and Git can be reviewed, repeated and rolled back.

2.title: What the Exam Asks: Application Delivery
2.text: Six pairs to keep apart. C I or C D: C I builds and tests, delivery reaches acceptance, and deployment reaches production. Push or pull: Git Ops agents pull the desired state and keep reconciling it. Rolling, blue green or canary: replace gradually, switch whole environments, or shift a share of traffic. Helm or Kustomize: templates and values in releases, or patches over a base. Tag or digest: a tag can move, and a digest cannot. And Argo C D or Flux, or Helm: Git Ops tools, or a package manager. Exam tip: ask what moves the change.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: To recap. For pipelines, C I builds and tests, delivery reaches acceptance, and deployment reaches production. For images, a tag can move, and a digest is a fixed hash. Git Ops is declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled, and continuously reconciled, and agents like Argo C D and Flux fix drift. The release strategies are recreate, rolling, blue green, canary, A B and shadow, and progressive delivery adds analysis. Helm charts and values make releases, and Kustomize bases and overlays patch Y A M L. And rollback is helm rollback, kube control rollout undo or a Git revert. Now ten practice questions.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Continuous delivery deploys changes automatically into an acceptance environment, with tests and a way to roll back. Continuous deployment carries finished software directly to production. C I is the build and test stage before both.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Harbor Books must be sure that staging and production run exactly the same image, even if someone pushes a different image under an existing tag. Which reference does that? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A digest identifies one version of an image and is immutable, while a tag can be moved to a different image. The latest tag can move, and a registry holds many images.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Which list gives the four Git Ops principles of the Open Git Ops project? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. The desired state must be declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically by software agents, and continuously reconciled with the actual state.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. In Git Ops, what does it mean that the desired state is pulled? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Software agents read the desired state from the state store whenever they need to, which makes continuous reconciliation possible. A pushed change happens once, and is not watched afterwards.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Someone changes the orders Deployment by hand in a cluster that an Argo C D or Flux agent manages from Git. What should happen? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Drift is the actual state moving away from the desired state. The agent keeps observing the cluster, and applies the desired state from Git again. Git stays the source of truth.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Which deployment strategy kills all the old Pods before it creates new ones, so that there is downtime? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The Recreate strategy stops every existing Pod first, and only then creates the new ones. The other strategies keep serving users with the old version while the new one comes up.

2.title: Practice Question 7
2.text: Question seven. Harbor Books wants to send a small share of visitors to a new storefront version, watch the results, and then increase the share or roll back. Which strategy is this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A canary shifts traffic gradually, so the team can observe the new version in production and roll back if needed. Blue green switches everything at once, and shadow releases copy requests without serving users from the new version.

2.title: Practice Question 8
2.text: Question eight. In Helm, what is a release? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A release is a chart installed in a cluster, and the same chart can be installed many times, each as its own release. The package is the chart, the shared collection is a repository, and the defaults live in values dot Y A M L.

2.title: Practice Question 9
2.text: Question nine. Which tool customizes plain Y A M L with a base and overlays, and is built into kube control? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Kustomize layers overlays with patches over a base of plain Y A M L, and kube control can build and apply the result. Helm uses templates, Flux is a Git Ops agent, and Argo Rollouts is for progressive delivery.

2.title: Practice Question 10
2.text: Question ten. A Helm upgrade of the Harbor Books database release misbehaves. Which command returns to an earlier revision? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. The rollback command takes the release name and a revision, and returns the release to that revision, adding a new revision to the history. Uninstall removes the release, and the other commands only deal with repositories and search.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are the answers at a glance. Question one, C: delivery reaches acceptance, and deployment goes on to production. Question two, A: a digest is an immutable hash. Question three, D: declarative, versioned, pulled, reconciled. Question four, B: an agent fetches the desired state. Question five, C: the agent reconciles the drift. Question six, B: recreate kills all old Pods first. Question seven, A: a canary shifts a share of traffic. Question eight, D: a release is a chart running in a cluster. Question nine, C: Kustomize patches plain Y A M L. Question ten, B: helm rollback with a revision.
